report.source_text: A routine follow-up CT scan after 6 months showed multiple (approximately 20 in number) new nodules up to 2 cm in size, scattered in both lungs with a lower lobar predominance (Fig. 1). An enhancing soft tissue nodule measuring 2 cm in size was seen at the right T4–5 intervertebral foramen (Fig. 2). There was erosion of the adjacent lamina and pedicle. This nodule was protruding into the spinal canal without any significant mass effect on the spinal cord. There was no associated lymphadenopathy in chest or abdomen.

report.source_text: Because a metastatic process was the primary concern, a thoracoscopic wedge excision of two of the peripheral lung nodules from different lobes was performed. On microscopy, an admixture of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils were seen in the affected lung tissue. Focal areas of fibrosis were present in areas of inflamed lung (Fig. 3). Gram, fungal and acid fast stains were negative for microorganisms (not shown). The possibility of inflammatory pseudotumor was considered on the initial pathology report, but considering the absence of abundant myofibroblasts, a final pathologic diagnosis of chronic pneumonitis was given.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 70-year-old male shipyard worker with prior history of unclassified dermal sarcoma (resected with negative margins) presented for routine 6-month follow-up CT scan. Imaging revealed multiple new pulmonary nodules (approximately 20, up to 2 cm in size, with lower lobar predominance) and an enhancing soft tissue nodule (2 cm) at the right T4–5 intervertebral foramen with erosion of adjacent lamina and pedicle, protruding into the spinal canal without mass effect. The patient remained asymptomatic with normal inflammatory markers. Thoracoscopic wedge excision of two peripheral lung nodules from different lobes was performed due to concern for metastatic disease. Pathology showed chronic pneumonitis with an admixture of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils with focal fibrosis; Gram, fungal, and acid-fast stains were negative for microorganisms. The initial pathology report considered inflammatory pseudotumor but rendered a final diagnosis of chronic pneumonitis due to absence of abundant myofibroblasts. However, the final clinical and radiological impression, based on the distribution pattern of multiple scattered pulmonary nodules in conjunction with the concomitant intervertebral foramen mass, was that of an inflammatory process resembling an inflammatory pseudotumor. No treatment was offered. Follow-up CT at 18 months showed complete resolution of all lung nodules and the intervertebral foramen lesion, with only a persistent bony defect remaining.
